Ivan III. Known as Ivan the Great, he transformed Moscow from a subordinate principality into the dominant power of Eastern Europe. Though less celebrated in the West than Peter the Great or Catherine, he deserves to rank with them as a founder of Russia, for while they modernized the state, Ivan created it as a unified political entity and liberated it from foreign domination.

The first pivotal act came around 1480 when he refused to pay tribute to the Golden Horde Khan. For two centuries, Moscow had been subordinate to the Mongol overlords. The Horde was fractured and declining, but Ivan's defiance was symbolically profound. Russia was free. This act of defiance became a foundational legend of Russian independence and national identity.

Ivan then set about consolidating power over the Russian lands. He conquered the Novgorod Republic in 1478, the wealthy trading city-state to the north, absorbing its territories and merchant wealth. He defeated rival principalities including Tver and Yaroslavl. He expanded Moscow's borders to the Urals in the east, to the White Sea in the north, and southward toward Crimea. Through marriage alliances and conquest, Moscow became the undisputed hegemon of Russian lands.

Institutionally and culturally, Ivan built a foundation that would endure. He commissioned the building of the Moscow Kremlin, the fortified city center that remains Russia's seat of power. Its white stone walls and cathedrals became the symbol of Moscow's might. He adopted the double-headed eagle as Moscow's emblem, claiming succession to the Roman and Byzantine empires. He married Sophia Palaiologina, niece of the last Byzantine emperor, positioning Moscow as the heir to Constantinople and Orthodox Christianity. He centralized the Orthodox Church under Moscow's authority, framing Moscow as the Third Rome—after Rome and Constantinople.

He declared himself Gosudar, a word meaning ruler or sovereign, a claim to absolute authority previously held only by the Khan. He created a centralized state apparatus and nobility system based on service to the crown. He left his successors a stable, unified, and territorially vast domain.

His great-grandson was Ivan IV, who would transform this foundation into an empire through terror. Later, Peter the Great built on Ivan's foundation of absolute state power. Ivan III is the threshold between the medieval Russian principalities and the early modern Russian state, the moment when Moscow became Russian and Russia became free.
